title: Arizona Lowered the Bar for Its English Fluency Test. Experts Say It Will Harm Students in the Long Run.
author: Rafael Carranza
summary: Rafael Carranza, reporting for ProPublica's Local Reporting Network with Arizona Luminaria, investigates why enrollment in Arizona's structured English immersion program collapsed this year. The answer is not a leap in student fluency but a decision by the state Department of Education to lower the score needed to pass AZELLA, the test that governs exit from the program. Carranza sets the change against a documented history: federal investigators found the 2006 to 2012 version of the test wrongly classified children as proficient, in violation of civil rights law, and two settlements followed, one of which required the state to raise the passing threshold. He also shows a methodological shortcut. The department skipped the step of norming the test on native English speakers in 2020, and when that check was belatedly run nearly half of the native speakers failed, a result driven partly by kindergarten and first grade test takers. Officials used that finding to justify a lower bar for English learners. Researchers quoted in the piece argue the test was never developed correctly and that there is no educational or research basis for the underlying English-only model.
points: The reported enrollment drop is an artifact of a changed cut score rather than of improved student fluency, which is the investigation's central finding.
Arizona has been here before, and the piece documents federal civil rights findings plus two settlements over exactly this pattern of premature reclassification.
The methodological detail is damning: the state skipped norming the test on native speakers, and when the check was finally run nearly half of them failed.
Officials then used a result shaped heavily by kindergarten and first grade native speakers to justify lowering the bar for English learners.
The piece surfaces a perverse funding incentive, since district money for English learners is tied to the number of students still enrolled in immersion.
quotes: The program is known as “structured English immersion,” or colloquially as “English-only” because all instruction is required to be in English. This limits their time for core subjects, like math and science, that are critical to academic success and college readiness. Arizona is the only state with English-only laws still in effect for its public schools.

But the number of students enrolled in the curriculum has tumbled dramatically this year. At the Tucson Unified School District, where Ramos teaches, the percentage of test-taking students who scored high enough to be classified as proficient in English more than doubled — from 10% in 2025 to 24% in 2026.

Rather than a big leap in fluency, however, the test results reflect the Arizona Department of Education lowering the grade needed to pass. The changes were approved by outgoing Superintendent of Public Instruction Tom Horne, a longtime Republican defender of Arizona’s English-only policies.

Experts warn this change will do lasting harm to tens of thousands of Arizona students who will exit the structured English immersion program before they know the language well enough to succeed. Such students are already part of the lowest-performing group on standardized tests, and the loss of specialized instruction could further harm their long-term academic success, according to education researchers.

Past attempts by the Arizona Department of Education to reclassify large numbers of children learning English as fluent prompted federal investigations by the departments of Justice and Education. Federal officials contended placing such students in classrooms where they struggled because they lacked knowledge of English violated their civil and educational rights, and Arizona agreed to a settlement more than a decade ago.

The U.S. departments of Justice and Education determined the version of AZELLA administered between 2006 and 2012 — coinciding with Horne’s first two terms as the state’s top education official — was “not a valid measure of English language proficiency and readiness.” As a result, the state had removed at least 28,000 students from structured English immersion who still lacked proficiency in reading and writing the language.

After the Arizona Department of Education lowered the score needed to pass the test, the statewide reclassification rate for 2026 jumped to 26%, according to the department’s official tally announced to teachers at a September training. Nearly 113,000 students took the 2026 AZELLA, according to the department, resulting in the reclassification of about 30,000 students as proficient and their removal from English-language services this school year.

English learners already lag far behind their peers, resulting in lower rates of graduation and postsecondary attainment. In 2025, standardized reading tests administered to all Arizona third graders showed a 31% disparity between English-language learners and other students, according to the Center for the Future of Arizona’s Education Progress Meter.
